key_insight: Predictive self-supervision in CT tends to preserve predictable anatomy better than diagnostically important but context-dependent pathology, creating a "predictability bias."
clinical_relevance: For medical imaging models, being easy to predict from surrounding anatomy is not the same as being clinically useful, so training goals should protect sparse pathology signals.
method: Trained TAP-JEPA, a ViT-B/3D joint-embedding predictive model, on 113,611 CT volumes.
Audited the model by replaying the exact masking, teacher, and predictor steps used in training.
Compared prediction effects on anatomy vs pathology using scan-level classification, Skill, teacher-direction shifts, and downstream probe margins.
evidence_signal: Across CT evaluation, prediction reduced mean Skill much more for pathology than anatomy (0.388→0.271 vs 0.921→0.873), and the model was competitive with COLIPRI, Merlin, and VoxelFM on scan-level classification.
watch_item: These findings come from CT data and model-specific audits, so the size of the bias may differ across modalities, datasets, and masking/training choices.
paper_title: The Predictability Bias of Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning in Medical Imaging
